hook.support: You apply for a job. The boss types your name into Google. What do they find? That is your brand. You can shape it.
hook.core: You apply for an apprenticeship. Before they call you, the boss searches your name. What comes up: a party pic from two years ago, or a profile that says who you are and what you can do? Whether you like it or not, you already have a personal brand. This course is about taking control of it.
hook.extend: A personal brand is the impression people form of you from what they can see: your profiles, posts and how you describe yourself. Employers, clients and customers look. Learning to shape that impression on purpose is a literacy skill: choosing words, layout and tone for an audience.

why.support: Bosses often look you up. A good profile can help you get the job.
why.core: Many employers check social media before they hire. A clear, honest profile helps you stand out for the right reasons.
why.extend: Your online presence is often your first impression. Writing it for a real audience and purpose is a skill you’ll use for every job, course or side hustle.

articles.title: You already have a brand

body.support:
Your **personal brand** is the picture people get of you. It comes from what they see online.

**Who looks?**
- bosses.
- customers.
- people you might work with.

**Check what they see.** Search your name. Look at your public posts. Set personal accounts to private.

**Write a profile.** A **profile** is a short page about you. It has:
- a clear photo.
- a **headline**: who you are.
- a few lines about you.
- your skills.
- how to contact you.

**Choose your words.** Think about your **audience**. A boss wants to know you are reliable. Show it.

- Not great: I’m a hard worker.
- Better: I’ve never missed a shift.
.
Keep your **tone** friendly and polite. Check your spelling.
body.core:
Your **personal brand** is the impression people get of you from what they can see: your profiles, posts and photos. Everyone has one. The question is whether you shape it.

**Who’s looking?** Employers, customers, clients, and people you might work with. In a 2018 US survey, 70% of employers said they check social media before hiring.

**Step 1: Check.** Search your name. Look at your public posts and photos as a boss would. Use **privacy settings** on personal accounts.

**Step 2: Build a profile.** Work **platforms** like LinkedIn or SEEK have a set layout:
- **photo:** clear, friendly, just you.
- **headline:** who you are, in a few words (“Year 12 student | Apprentice carpenter in training”).
- **about:** two or three sentences about you and what you want.
- **skills and experience:** jobs, sport, volunteering, certificates.
- **contact:** a sensible email.

**Step 3: Choose your words for your audience.**
- Give proof, not claims. “I’ve never missed a shift” beats “I’m a hard worker”.
- Use action words: led, built, served, fixed.
- Match the **tone** to the platform. LinkedIn is professional. An Instagram page for a side hustle can be more relaxed.
- Be honest. Everything should be true in an interview.
body.extend:
Your **personal brand** is the impression others form of you from what they can find: profiles, posts, photos and how you describe yourself. You can’t opt out of having one, but you can shape it.

**Audience.** Employers, clients and customers all look. In a 2018 US survey of hiring managers, 70% said they use social media to screen candidates. Of those, 57% had found something that led them not to hire someone.

**Audit.** Search your name, check what’s public, and use **privacy settings** on personal accounts.

**Layout and structure.** Professional **platforms** use a fixed structure, so readers can scan:
- **photo:** clear and appropriate.
- **headline:** role and goal in a few words.
- **about:** a short summary in your own voice.
- **experience and skills:** paid work, volunteering, sport, certificates.
- **contact:** a professional email.

**Language choices.** Every word should suit the audience and purpose:
- evidence over claims: “trained three new staff” beats “great leader”.
- action verbs and specific numbers.
- a **tone** that fits the platform: formal on LinkedIn, more relaxed for a side-hustle page, never careless.
- honesty: anything you claim may be tested in an interview.

The same person might write three versions: one for an employer, one for clients, and one for friends.

caseStudies.title: The boss is looking

body.support:
In **2018**, a US jobs website called **CareerBuilder** did a survey. More than **1,000** bosses who hire people answered it.

**70%** of them said they look at social media to check people who apply for jobs.

Some found things that made them say no. Others liked what they saw.

This survey was in the US. But Australian bosses can look you up too.

What would a boss find about you?
body.core:
In **2018**, the US jobs website **CareerBuilder** surveyed **1,012** hiring managers. The Harris Poll ran the survey.

**70%** said they use social media to research job candidates.

Of those who did, **57%** had found something that made them decide **not** to hire someone.

The survey was done in the United States. Australian employers aren’t counted in it. But anyone can search your name, here or anywhere.

So it pays to check what’s public, and to give employers something good to find.
body.extend:
In **2018**, the US jobs site **CareerBuilder** commissioned The Harris Poll to survey **1,012** hiring and HR managers.

**70%** said they use social networking sites to research job candidates. Of those, **57%** said they had found content that caused them not to hire a candidate.

The survey was in the United States, so it doesn’t tell us exactly what Australian employers do. Its results also depend on what managers chose to report.

Still, the lesson travels. A personal brand is built from what’s visible. Two moves follow: limit what shouldn’t be public, and create something worth finding.

source.name: WTOP News — “Clean up your ‘digital dirt’; bosses check your social media profiles” (August 2018, reporting a CareerBuilder survey)

teacher.overview: A VM 3&4 induction course. Students learn what a personal brand is, check their own online presence, analyse the layout of a work profile (photo, headline, about, experience and skills, contact), and choose language for an audience and platform (evidence over claims, action verbs, tone). They write a profile for a job, apprenticeship or side hustle. The case study is a 2018 CareerBuilder survey: 70% of US hiring managers said they research candidates on social media.
prep: Students don’t need to log in to real platforms; the profile can be written in the workbook.
Be ready for sensitive discoveries when students search their own names; have the eSafety Commissioner page handy.

**Sort (10 min):** keep it or change it.
**Case study (10 min):** the boss is looking.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Write the profile
steps: **Check & reflect (10 min):** quick check, reflection, sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 photo (first impression); 2 headline (role and goal); 3 about (own voice, short); 4 experience as proof; 5 current skills; 6 professional contact.

**Sort:** keep — the clear headline; deck photos (proof of skills). Change or hide — old party photo (make private); silly email; rude comment about a boss (delete); “best worker ever!!!” (claim, not proof).

**Case study:** 70% of 1,012 US hiring managers said they research candidates on social media; 57% of those had found content that led them not to hire. It is a US survey, so it doesn’t directly describe Australian employers.

resources.label: WTOP — bosses check your social media (2018 CareerBuilder survey)

realityCheck: **Self-searches can turn up upsetting things** (old posts, images shared by others). Have a private follow-up plan and the eSafety reporting link ready.
**Not every student wants an online presence.** That’s a valid choice. The profile can live in the workbook or a resume.
**The survey is American.** The course says so; use it to talk about checking where evidence comes from.
**Works in a real class:** yes. The “proof, not claims” rewrite is the moment it clicks.

levels.support: Aimed at about Years 3–4 reading: shorter article and case study, 5 key words, word bank and a profile frame.
levels.core: Aimed at about Years 5–6 reading: the standard version with checking, layout, language choices and tone.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 7 and up: audience analysis, survey limits, multiple versions for different audiences.
